account: At Stanford University, a participant with bulbar-onset amyotrophic lateral sclerosis took part in the BrainGate2 trial. News reports identify her as Pat Bennett, 68. Stanford's release dates her surgery to 29 March 2022, when four 64-electrode arrays went into ventral premotor cortex (area 6v) and area 44. The release says that research sessions began about a month after the surgery. A recurrent neural network converted her neural activity into phoneme probabilities, and a 125,000-word language model assembled sentences. She produced text at 62 words per minute. The word error rate was 9.1% on a 50-word vocabulary and 23.8% on the full vocabulary. The paper dates sessions by post-implant day (119, 136 and 141 for the reported data) and gives no calendar dates. The Stanford release says that 62 words per minute came after four months, which places the result in about August 2022. Willett and colleagues reported the results in Nature on 23 August 2023. The team described the work as a proof of concept in research sessions. In a Nature commentary of the same day, Nick Ramsey and Nathan Crone, who were not part of the study, called this result and the result from the University of California, San Francisco, a turning point for restoring communication. On 14 August 2025 a Stanford-led team reported in Cell that she took part in later inner-speech decoding sessions from post-implant day 412 to day 995. Real-time decoding of her imagined sentences on a 50-word vocabulary reached a 24% word error rate. The authors report that she still communicated mainly with a writing board or an iPad.

ai_role.statement: An RNN decoder plus an n-gram language model is the mechanism translating neural activity into text. The Stanford neurosurgeon describes the language model as “a sophisticated auto-correct”. The benefit is attributable to the decoding system.

fields.account: At Stanford University, a participant with bulbar-onset amyotrophic lateral sclerosis took part in the BrainGate2 trial. News reports identify her as Pat Bennett, 68. Stanford's release dates her surgery to 29 March 2022, when four 64-electrode arrays went into ventral premotor cortex (area 6v) and area 44. The release says that research sessions began about a month after the surgery. A recurrent neural network converted her neural activity into phoneme probabilities, and a 125,000-word language model assembled sentences. She produced text at 62 words per minute. The word error rate was 9.1% on a 50-word vocabulary and 23.8% on the full vocabulary. The paper dates sessions by post-implant day (119, 136 and 141 for the reported data) and gives no calendar dates. The Stanford release says that 62 words per minute came after four months, which places the result in about August 2022. Willett and colleagues reported the results in Nature on 23 August 2023. The team described the work as a proof of concept in research sessions. In a Nature commentary of the same day, Nick Ramsey and Nathan Crone, who were not part of the study, called this result and the result from the University of California, San Francisco, a turning point for restoring communication. On 14 August 2025 a Stanford-led team reported in Cell that she took part in later inner-speech decoding sessions from post-implant day 412 to day 995. Real-time decoding of her imagined sentences on a 50-word vocabulary reached a 24% word error rate. The authors report that she still communicated mainly with a writing board or an iPad.
